facts.claim: In a lifespan study of 145 people (ages 8-79), tapping got steadier from childhood into adulthood. The authors fitted a cubic curve of tapping variability (SD of inter-tap intervals, ms) against age in years. Plugging in ages gives about 51 ms at 8, 44 ms at 10, 39 ms at 12, 34 ms at 14, 29 ms at 16, 26 ms at 18 and 22 ms at 20.
facts.figure: Y = 84.90 - 5.166*X + 0.122*X^2 - 0.001*X^3 (X = age in years). The cubic model explained 42.6% of variance, F(3,142) = 34.71, p < .001. Evaluated values (our arithmetic, re-checked): 50.9 / 44.4 / 38.8 / 33.7 / 29.4 / 25.6 / 22.4 ms at ages 8/10/12/14/16/18/20. The pacing stimulus was a repeated snare-drum sound at 500 ms and 667 ms ISI (90 and 120 bpm).
facts.source_title: Thompson, White-Schwoch, Tierney & Kraus (2015) Beat Synchronization across the Lifespan: Intersection of Development and Musical Experience. PLoS ONE 10(6): e0128839
facts.caveat: Verified: the equation, R^2 and the SD-of-inter-tap-interval definition all appear in the text. The stimulus was a prerecorded snare-drum sound, not a metronome. The curve was fitted across the whole 8-79 age range, and the -0.001 cubic coefficient is rounded. These are model-fitted values, not group means. The Fig 3 caption gives slightly different coefficients (85.055, -5.192, .123, -.001), which change the values by under 1 ms in the 8-20 range. The sample mixes musicians and non-musicians. Guitar onset detection adds jitter, so the comparison favours the study's participants. MEASURE MISMATCH: the study used SD of inter-tap intervals; the app's spreadMs is SD of asynchrony. Treat the band as approximate and keep the bands wide.

facts.claim: The age groups in the lifespan study were children 8-13 (mean 11.0, n=27), adolescents 14-17 (16.4, n=32), young adults 18-21 (20.3, n=18), middle-aged adults 22-42 (28.5, n=25) and older adults 51-79 (63.7, n=43). Tapping consistency improved into adulthood and became more variable again in older adults.
facts.figure: N = 145. Group means 11.04 / 16.38 / 20.25 / 28.49 / 63.67 years. Age main effect on variability F(4,141) = 21.58, p < .001.
facts.source_title: Thompson et al. (2015) Beat Synchronization across the Lifespan, PLoS ONE 10(6): e0128839
facts.caveat: Cross-sectional design. In the abstract the 'improves into adulthood' and 'older adulthood ... more variable' clauses are separate fragments of one sentence, so quote only one fragment.

facts.claim: In the same lifespan study, a larger share of life spent playing music went with steadier tapping and smaller asynchrony. Musicians were less variable than non-musicians, and the within-group difference was significant among adolescents and middle-aged adults.
facts.figure: Variability vs proportion of life playing music: R(100) = -.255, p = .011. Asynchrony: R(100) = -.241, p = .016. Musician main effect on variability: F(1,101) = 7.698, p = .007. Within-group variability differences: adolescents p = .012, middle-aged adults p = .01.
facts.source_title: Thompson et al. (2015) Beat Synchronization across the Lifespan, PLoS ONE 10(6): e0128839
facts.caveat: Correlational. Older adults were excluded from the music-experience analyses.

facts.claim: In 166 online adults tapping on a laptop to a metronome (measured with the REPP platform, about 2 ms system latency and jitter), the average SD of asynchrony was about 41 ms. When tapping to music it was about 43 ms. More self-reported musical training went with less variable tapping.
facts.figure: Metronome (isochronous): SD of asynchrony M = 40.68 ms (between-person SD 11.98). Music: M = 42.68 ms (SD 15.82). Correlation of tapping variability with musical training r = -.32, p < .001 (N = 226 for this correlation).
facts.source_title: Anglada-Tort, Harrison & Jacoby (2022) REPP: A robust cross-platform solution for online sensorimotor synchronization experiments. Behavior Research Methods
facts.caveat: Participants tapped on a laptop rather than playing an instrument. The experiment is labelled Experiment 3 in one place and Experiment 2 in another. The training correlation used a larger sample (N = 226) than the test-retest sample (N = 166). Guitar onset detection adds jitter. Same measure as the app's spreadMs (SD of asynchrony).

facts.claim: Fifteen professional drummers played a drum-kit pattern with a metronome at 60, 120 and 200 bpm. Their mean timing error was tiny. At 60 and 120 bpm the hi-hat hand was about 2 ms off, while snare and bass drum were about 10 ms early. At 200 bpm the hi-hat hand was about 10 ms late and the other limbs about 1 ms off. The absolute errors were smaller than in earlier tapping studies.
facts.figure: Mean synchronization error ~2 ms (right hand, hi-hat) and ~-10 ms (left hand snare, right foot bass) at 60/120 bpm. At 200 bpm the right hand was ~+10 ms and the others ~1 ms.
facts.source_title: Fujii, Hirashima, Kudo, Ohtsuki, Nakamura & Oda (2011) Synchronization error of drum kit playing with a metronome at different tempi by professional drummers. Music Perception 28(5): 491-503
facts.caveat: Verified against the official abstract on the Keio University research portal; the original Kansai repo URL returned 503. The abstract also says 'the right hand (highhat cymbals) showed small mean SE (~2 ms)'. The players were pros on a drum kit. App latency calibration errors directly shift meanErrMs, so only use when the user has a recent latency calibration.

facts.claim: When adults tap to a metronome they typically tap slightly early (negative mean asynchrony). In finger-tapping experiments this is typically -20 to -100 ms. In 61 young adults (22-35) from the Human Connectome Project the mean was -55 ms for hand taps and -105 ms for foot taps.
facts.figure: Typical SMA -20 to -100 ms (citing Aschersleben 2002); study mean -55 ms (hands), -105 ms (feet); N = 61, HCP1200 MEG motor task
facts.source_title: Michalareas, Grabenhorst & Sun (2022) Tuning in Sensorimotor Synchronization. bioRxiv 10.1101/2022.12.16.520727
facts.caveat: Preprint. Other sources give smaller adult values (~10 ms, see tba-08), so treat the magnitude as a range. Tapping on a surface differs from plucking a string.

facts.claim: Adults often anticipate the beat slightly (about 10 ms, per one cited study). This anticipation (negative asynchrony) is rarely found in young children.
facts.figure: Adult negative asynchrony ~10 ms (Miyake et al., 2004, as cited)
facts.source_title: Bobin-Bègue, Droit-Volet & Provasi (2014) Young children's difficulties in switching from rhythm production to temporal interval production (>1 s). Frontiers in Psychology 5:1346
facts.caveat: Adult magnitudes disagree across sources (~10 ms here vs -20 to -100 ms in tba-07). Secondary citation.

facts.claim: Spontaneous (natural) tapping tempo slows with age. Children aged 2-7 tap at an inter-tap interval of about 400-500 ms (about 120-150 bpm), slowing to about 600 ms (about 100 bpm) in early adulthood. How variable that natural tempo is also decreases with age.
facts.figure: Children 2-7 yrs: ITI 400-500 ms (~120-150 bpm). Early adulthood: ~600 ms (~100 bpm).
facts.source_title: Bobin-Bègue, Droit-Volet & Provasi (2014), Frontiers in Psychology 5:1346, citing Drake et al. 2000; Provasi & Bobin-Bègue 2003; McAuley et al. 2006
facts.caveat: Secondary summary of several primary studies. The paper also states 'the variability (SD) of SMT decreases with age'. Tempo flavour only, not a skill judgement.

facts.claim: In Hungarian schoolchildren, the average spontaneous motor tempo was about 116 bpm in first grade and about 115 bpm in third grade (mean age 8.9). The authors note that adults average about 100 bpm.
facts.figure: SMT 115.63 bpm (SD 26.27) in 1st grade; 114.68 bpm (SD 38.31) in 3rd grade; adult average ca. 100 bpm
facts.source_title: First school year tapping predicts children's third-grade literacy skills. Scientific Reports (2023)
facts.caveat: N = 37, a single cohort. Third-grade mean age is 8.9; first grade was about a year earlier. Tempo flavour only.

facts.claim: In 3-4-year-olds (mean 4.4 years) asked to drum along with an experimenter at 2.5 Hz and 1.67 Hz (150 and 100 bpm), 22 of 35 children (about 63%) synchronized at both rates. The other 13 synchronized at neither.
facts.figure: 22/35 synchronizers (~63%), 13/35 non-synchronizers (~37%); ages 3-4, mean 4.37 years (SD 0.51)
facts.source_title: Woodruff Carr, White-Schwoch, Tierney, Strait & Kraus (2014) Beat synchronization predicts neural speech encoding and reading readiness in preschoolers. PNAS 111(40): 14559-14564
facts.caveat: Drumming with a live partner, not a metronome. Percentages computed from the counts.

facts.claim: Even 10-year-olds do not tap to an auditory rhythm as consistently as adults, and the range of tempos 8-year-olds comfortably tap at is not as wide as adults'.
facts.figure: Ages 8 and 10 vs adults (qualitative; Drake, Jones & Baruch 2000 as cited)
facts.source_title: Cirelli, Bosnyak, Manning, Spinelli, Marie, Fujioka, Ghahremani & Trainor (2014) Beat-induced fluctuations in auditory cortical beta-band activity: using EEG to measure age-related changes. Frontiers in Psychology 5:742
facts.caveat: Secondary citation. The sentence continues '...as consistently as do adults'.

facts.claim: First-graders tapping to a metronome had an average absolute asynchrony of about 0.15 of the beat interval at 120 and 150 bpm (about 78 ms at 120 bpm). By third grade (mean age 8.9) it had dropped to about 0.09 of the beat at 120 bpm (about 45 ms) and about 0.065 at 150 bpm (about 26 ms).
facts.figure: Absolute asynchrony as a proportion of the beat interval. 1st grade: 0.157 (SD 0.068) at 120 bpm, 0.147 (SD 0.068) at 150 bpm. 3rd grade: 0.091 (SD 0.058) at 120 bpm, 0.065 (SD 0.038) at 150 bpm. The ms values are our conversions.
facts.source_title: First school year tapping predicts children's third-grade literacy skills. Scientific Reports (2023)
facts.caveat: Mean ABSOLUTE tap-to-beat difference divided by the beat interval, so it is not comparable with the signed meanErrMs. N = 37, Hungarian cohort.

facts.claim: Musicians (at least 6 years of private lessons, mean 10 years) tapping a familiar melody at their own natural rate had a coefficient of variation of 0.05. Non-musicians had 0.06. In a separate study (more than 6 years of instruction vs 2 years or less), musicians' CV was 0.045 and non-musicians' 0.064.
facts.figure: CV at spontaneous rate: musicians 0.05 vs non-musicians 0.06 (Scheurich et al. 2018, N = 20+20, tapping 'Mary Had a Little Lamb'). Musicians 0.045 (SE .0017) vs non-musicians 0.064 (SE .0033) (Tranchant et al. 2022, N = 28+28, ages 18-35).
facts.source_title: Scheurich, Zamm & Palmer (2018) Tapping Into Rate Flexibility. Frontiers in Psychology 9:458; Tranchant, Scholler & Palmer (2022) Endogenous rhythms influence musicians' and non-musicians' interpersonal synchrony. Scientific Reports 12:12973
facts.caveat: Inter-onset-interval CVs during self-paced melody tapping, not metronome asynchrony SD. Use cautiously and phrase as 'in a self-paced tapping study'.

facts.claim: When pairs of people tapped a melody together in a duet, musician pairs were a median of about 24 ms apart from each other and non-musician pairs about 34 ms apart.
facts.figure: Median absolute asynchrony: musicians 23.94 ms vs non-musicians 33.68 ms (U = 150, p < .01); 28 musicians + 28 non-musicians
facts.source_title: Tranchant, Scholler & Palmer (2022) Endogenous rhythms influence musicians' and non-musicians' interpersonal synchrony. Scientific Reports 12:12973
facts.caveat: Partner-to-partner duet tapping, not a fixed metronome. The app's meanErrMs is signed, so do not use it directly.

facts.claim: Trained musicians can synchronize with beats as fast as 100-120 ms apart (about 500-600 events per minute, e.g. fast subdivisions). At the slow end, intervals longer than about 1.8 s (about 33 bpm) make synchronization inaccurate.
facts.figure: Fastest IOI ~100-120 ms (trained musicians); slow limit ~1800 ms
facts.source_title: Rajendran, Teki & Schnupp (2018) Temporal Processing in Audition: Insights from Music. Neuroscience 389: 4-18
facts.caveat: Both limits appear in this review, summarizing Repp's work. Bobin-Bègue et al. 2014 also cite ~1800 ms for adults, but 1.5 s for 5-year-olds.

facts.claim: Tapping variability during synchronization is greater in children than in adults, and the variability of natural tapping tempo decreases with age.
facts.figure: Qualitative (Repp 2005; Drake et al. 2000; McAuley et al. 2006 as cited)
facts.source_title: Bobin-Bègue, Droit-Volet & Provasi (2014), Frontiers in Psychology 5:1346
facts.caveat: Qualitative only.

facts.claim: Guinness World Records reported that John Taylor ('Dr Hot Licks') played 'Flight of the Bumblebee' at 620 bpm on New Year 2012 at Olympian City mall in Kowloon, Hong Kong. That beat the previous record of 600 bpm. The piece is written in semiquavers (16th notes).

facts.source_title: Guinness World Records news: Dr Hot Licks sees in the New Year in Hong Kong with new fastest guitar-playing record (9 Jan 2012)
facts.caveat: Call it 'a 2012 Guinness record', not 'the current record'. The record is 16th notes at 620 bpm, so it is not the same unit as lesson BPM.

facts.claim: Before his record attempt, Dr Hot Licks warmed up by playing first at 250 bpm and then at 400 bpm.

facts.source_title: Fender press release via PR Newswire: 'Guitar Isn't Dead: Research Shows Learning to Play Helps Us Live Better Lives' (16 Oct 2018)
facts.caveat: Company figure with no published method. Phrase as 'Fender found'.

facts.claim: Fender surveyed 500 aspiring and beginning players in the US and UK. Nearly half of beginners said they quit learning an instrument because of time constraints, and 33 percent said they were not growing skills fast enough or as fast as they expected.

facts.claim: The Fender release says neuroscientist Daniel Levitin advised that the best way to learn is playing your favourite songs for 5 minutes a day, every day, at the same time of day, rather than two hours on one day. Levitin is quoted directly: playing even five minutes a day can bring physical, mental and emotional benefits.

facts.claim: In Fender's survey, 72 percent of respondents picked up guitar to gain a life skill or as a means of self-betterment, 61 percent to learn songs to play alone or socially, and 46 percent to make music with others.

facts.claim: Django Reinhardt received a banjo-guitar at 12. On the night of 2 November 1928 a fire in his wagon badly burned the ring and little fingers of his left hand. Doctors believed he would never play again, but he went on to play solos mainly with his index and middle fingers.

facts.claim: Tony Iommi lost the tips of the middle and ring fingers of his fretting hand in a factory accident at 17. A Django Reinhardt record inspired him to keep going. facts.source_title: Wikipedia: Tony Iommi
facts.caveat: Say washing-up liquid bottle. He is left-handed, so his fretting hand is his right hand.

facts.claim: In a finger-tapping sequence study, a night of sleep after practice was followed by about 20% faster typing of the sequence with no loss of accuracy. The same amount of time awake gave no significant benefit.
facts.figure: ~20% increase in motor speed after a night of sleep; wake: no significant benefit (Harvard Gazette: about 2% for the group retested 12 h later without sleep)
facts.source_title: Walker, Brakefield, Morgan, Hobson & Stickgold (2002). Practice with sleep makes perfect: sleep-dependent motor skill learning. Neuron 35(1):205-211
facts.caveat: Abstract confirmed via search-indexed copies (PubMed blocked fetch). The 2% wake figure is from the Harvard Gazette. Sleep-specific effect disputed (Pan & Rickard 2015, ps-sleep-meta-caveat).

facts.claim: After one night of sleep, finger-sequence speed improved 17.0% and errors fell 34.5%. After three nights, speed was up 26.2% and errors down 48.3% overall.
facts.figure: Night 1: +17.0% speed, -34.5% error rate (n=10). After 3 nights (72 h): +26.2% speed, -48.3% error rate (n=10). Versus one night these were only trends (speed P = 0.07, errors P = 0.10).
facts.source_title: Walker et al. (2003). Sleep and the time course of motor skill learning. Learning & Memory 10(4):275-284
facts.caveat: Groups of 10. Sleep effect disputed (Pan & Rickard 2015). Keyboard finger-tapping.

facts.claim: Within a single training session of 12 short trials, learners got 52% faster and made 47% fewer errors on a new finger sequence.
facts.figure: +7.8 sequences (52%) speed and -47% error rate across 12 training trials (n=40, averaged across groups)
facts.source_title: Walker et al. (2003). Sleep and the time course of motor skill learning. Learning & Memory 10(4):275-284
facts.caveat: Keyboard sequence task, not guitar.

facts.claim: Doubling practice in a day did not increase the overnight improvement: one session gave +17.0% speed overnight and two sessions gave +17.5%, a difference that was not significant.
facts.figure: Overnight speed gain 17.0% (one session) vs 17.5% (two sessions); between-group P = 0.77
facts.source_title: Walker et al. (2003). Sleep and the time course of motor skill learning. Learning & Memory 10(4):275-284
facts.caveat: n=10 per group, single finger-tapping task.

facts.claim: People who napped at midday after practising a finger sequence improved 16% at later testing. A group that did not nap improved by a non-significant 3.8%.
facts.figure: Nap group +16% (3.5 seq/trial, p = 0.002, n=14, average nap 67 min); no-nap group +3.8% (n.s., n=12)
facts.source_title: Nishida & Walker (2007). Daytime naps, motor memory consolidation and regionally specific sleep spindles. PLoS ONE 2(4):e341
facts.caveat: Small sample (26). Sleep-effect dispute applies.

facts.claim: In early learning of a new skill, nearly all the improvement showed up across short 10-second rest breaks, not during the practice itself. That early phase made up about 95% of the first day's learning.
facts.figure: 10 s practice / 10 s rest, 36 trials on Day 1; early learning (to ~trial 11) = ~95% of Day-1 learning; micro-online changes ~nil; n=27
facts.source_title: Bönstrup et al. (2019). A rapid form of offline consolidation in skill learning. Current Biology 29(8):1346-1351
facts.caveat: Early learning of a new keyboard sequence only. Say 'nearly all early learning'.

facts.claim: A large online replication (cumulative N = 951 across experiments) confirmed that early skill gains happen during short rests and are not just recovery from fatigue.
facts.figure: Cumulative N = 951; first replication experiment N = 389; 10 s practice / 10 s rest, 36 trials
facts.source_title: Bönstrup, Iturrate, Hebart, Censor & Cohen (2020). Mechanisms of offline motor learning at a microscale of seconds in large-scale crowdsourced data. npj Science of Learning 5:7
facts.caveat: Keyboard sequence task; early learning only.

facts.claim: A mathematical analysis of learning in models found that the training 'sweet spot' is getting about 85% right (about 15.87% errors).
facts.figure: Optimal error rate ~15.87%; optimal training accuracy ~85%
facts.source_title: Wilson, Shenhav, Straccia & Cohen (2019). The Eighty Five Percent Rule for optimal learning. Nature Communications 10:4646
facts.caveat: Theoretical result for model learners (perceptron, neural nets, simulated monkey model), not tested on humans.

facts.claim: A meta-analysis found that focusing on the effect of a movement (the sound, the target) rather than on your body parts improves performance, with a moderate benefit for learning.
facts.figure: Performance g = 0.264 (73 studies, 1,824 participants); retention g = 0.583; transfer g = 0.584 (learning: 40 studies, 1,274 participants)
facts.source_title: Chua, Jimenez-Diaz, Lewthwaite, Kim & Wulf (2021). Superiority of external attentional focus for motor performance and learning: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Psychological Bulletin 147(6):618-645
facts.caveat: Small to moderate effects; mostly sport and balance tasks. '100+ studies' is approximate.

facts.claim: Mixing different skills in practice (random order) instead of drilling one at a time gave a medium benefit for transferring motor skills to new situations.
facts.figure: Overall SMD = 0.55 (34 studies in meta-analysis); adults 18-60 SMD = 0.54; older adults (60+) SMD = 1.28; participants under 18 SMD = 0.12 (negligible)
facts.source_title: Czyż, Wójcik & Solarská (2024). The effect of contextual interference on transfer in motor learning - a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychology 15:1377122
facts.caveat: Lab effect significant (0.75); applied-setting effect small and not significant (0.34).

facts.claim: When postal workers learned to type, the group practising one hour once a day learned most efficiently, and the group doing two 2-hour sessions a day learned least efficiently.
facts.figure: Four groups; sessions of 1 or 2 h, once or twice a day. Best: 1 x 1 h/day; worst: 2 x 2 h/day. ~30% speed loss at 1-9 month retention tests
facts.source_title: Baddeley & Longman (1978). The influence of length and frequency of training session on the rate of learning to type. Ergonomics 21(8):627-635
facts.caveat: Confirmed from abstract summaries; full text not read.

facts.claim: In musicians learning a 9-note keyboard sequence over three sessions spaced 5 min, 6 h or 24 h apart, sleep-spaced practice was linked to better accuracy, while speed gains came from both wake and sleep spacing.
facts.figure: 29 non-pianist musicians; spacing 5 min vs 6 h vs 24 h
facts.source_title: Simmons (2011). Distributed practice and procedural memory consolidation in musicians' skill learning. Journal of Research in Music Education 59(4):357-368
facts.caveat: From a secondary abstract summary. Small sample.

facts.claim: In a study of 17 advanced pianists learning a short concerto passage, how well they played it the next day was predicted by how they practised, especially how they handled errors, not by how long they practised.
facts.figure: 17 graduate/advanced undergraduate pianists; 3-measure excerpt of Shostakovich Piano Concerto No. 1; tested ~24 h later
facts.source_title: Duke, Simmons & Cash (2009). It's not how much; it's how: Characteristics of practice behavior and retention of performance skills. Journal of Research in Music Education 56(4):310-321
facts.caveat: Correlational, small sample, from secondary summaries.

facts.claim: In the classic violinist study, the best academy violinists had practised alone about 7,410 hours by age 18, versus 5,301 hours for good violinists and 3,420 for less accomplished ones. A 2019 replication found practice explained less of the difference (26% vs 48%).
facts.figure: 1993: best 7,410 h; good 5,301 h; less accomplished 3,420 h by age 18 (n=30). 2019 replication (n=39): best ~8,224 h, good ~9,844 h, less accomplished ~4,558 h; 26% variance explained vs original 48%.
facts.source_title: Macnamara & Maitra (2019). The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Römer (1993). Royal Society Open Science
facts.caveat: Retrospective self-estimates. In the replication 'good' practised more than 'best', so hours alone don't make an expert.

facts.claim: In a study of people building a new daily habit, it took on average 66 days for it to become automatic (range 18 to a projected 254 days). Missing a single day did not significantly harm habit formation.
facts.figure: 66 days average; range 18-254 days (254 extrapolated); 96 volunteers, 84-day study
facts.source_title: Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts & Wardle (2010). How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology 40(6):998-1009
facts.caveat: 66 days from participants whose data fit the model well. 254 is extrapolated. Simple daily health behaviours.

facts.claim: Across 24 experiments (475 people, 7,910 learning series), individual learning curves were best described by an exponential curve. Big early gains are followed by smaller and smaller ones, so slowing progress is the normal shape of learning, not failure.
facts.figure: 40 data sets, 7,910 learning series, 475 subjects, 24 experiments; exponential fit better than power in all unaveraged data sets
facts.source_title: Heathcote, Brown & Mewhort (2000). The power law repealed: The case for an exponential law of practice. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 7(2):185-207
facts.caveat: Counts from repository record and abstract; full paper not read.

facts.claim: A normal resting heart rate for adults (and children 10+) is 60 to 100 beats per minute.
facts.figure: 60-100 beats per minute (age 10+ and adults, at rest)
facts.source_title: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Pulse

facts.claim: Well-trained athletes often have resting heart rates of 40 to 60 beats per minute.
facts.figure: 40-60 beats per minute
facts.source_title: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Pulse

facts.claim: Normal resting heart rate ranges for children: ages 1-2: 80-130 bpm; 3-4: 80-120; 5-6: 75-115; 7-9: 70-110 (infants 1-11 months: 80-160).
facts.figure: 1-2 yrs 80-130; 3-4 yrs 80-120; 5-6 yrs 75-115; 7-9 yrs 70-110; infants 1-11 months 80-160 beats per minute
facts.source_title: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Pulse
facts.caveat: Ranges overlap.

facts.claim: A resting adult breathes about 12 to 18 times per minute.
facts.figure: 12-18 breaths per minute
facts.source_title: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Vital signs
facts.caveat: Many secondary sources quote 12-20; use the MedlinePlus 12-18 figure.

facts.claim: Estimated max heart rate is 220 minus age; target exercise zone is 50-85% of that, e.g. 95-162 bpm (max 190) for a 30-year-old.
facts.figure: Max HR ~ 220 - age; age 30: max 190 bpm, target zone 95-162 bpm
facts.source_title: University of Iowa Health Care: Target heart rate for exercise
facts.caveat: UIHC cites an AHA estimate; AHA page not fetched. 220-age is rough.

facts.claim: In 21-40 year olds, walking at about 100 steps per minute marks moderate intensity (3 METs) and about 130 steps/min marks vigorous intensity (6 METs).
facts.figure: Regression-optimal thresholds 102 and 129 steps/min (ROC models: 96 and 120); heuristic values 100 and 130 steps/min
facts.source_title: Tudor-Locke et al. 2019, Walking cadence (steps/min) and intensity in 21-40 year olds: CADENCE-adults, Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act 16:8 (PMID 30654810)
facts.caveat: 100/130 are rounded heuristics.

facts.claim: Elite runners at the 2016 IAU 100 km World Championship averaged 182 steps per minute (range 155-203).
facts.figure: mean 182.0 spm, range 155.4-203.1 spm (n=20)
facts.source_title: Burns, Zendler, Zernicke 2019, Step frequency patterns of elite ultramarathon runners during a 100-km road race, J Appl Physiol (PMID 30543498)

facts.claim: In Canadian Armed Forces drill, quick time is 120 paces per minute, slow time 60, and double time 180.
facts.figure: quick 120, slow 60, double 180 paces per minute
facts.source_title: Canadian Armed Forces Manual of Drill and Ceremonial, Chapter 3
facts.caveat: Attribute to the Canadian Armed Forces manual only.

facts.claim: In Canadian drill, light infantry and rifle regiments may quick-march at 140 paces per minute on their own parades.
facts.figure: 140 paces per minute
facts.source_title: Canadian Armed Forces Manual of Drill and Ceremonial, Chapter 3
facts.caveat: Only on those regiments' own parades, when ordered.

facts.claim: Dolbear's law (1897): temperature in F = cricket chirps in 15 seconds + 40, so chirps per minute = 4 x (F - 40); e.g. 120 chirps/min at about 70 F.
facts.figure: T(F) = chirps per 15 s + 40
facts.source_title: NOAA Office of Education: Can crickets tell temperature? The answer is in their chirp
facts.caveat: Species not identified by Dolbear (likely snowy tree cricket); species and local factors differ.

facts.claim: A hummingbird's heart beats 500-600 times a minute at rest, up to about 1000 in extreme conditions; 1260 beats a minute has been recorded in the Blue-throated Hummingbird.
facts.figure: 500-600 bpm resting; up to 1000 bpm; 1260 bpm recorded (Blue-throated Hummingbird)
facts.source_title: Virtual Museum of Canada / Musee de la nature et des sciences: A bird with a big heart
facts.caveat: Museum educational page; figures vary by species.

facts.claim: Hovering Anna's hummingbirds beat their wings about 44 times per second (~2650 per minute).
facts.figure: 44.2 +/- 1.8 Hz (six Anna's hummingbirds, Calypte anna); 44.2 x 60 = ~2652 per minute
facts.source_title: Hightower et al. 2021, How oscillating aerodynamic forces explain the timbre of the hummingbird's hum, eLife

facts.claim: Excised domestic cat larynges produced purr-range sounds with fundamental frequencies of 25-30 Hz (1500-1800 vibrations per minute) without neural input.
facts.source_title: Herbst et al. 2023, Domestic cat larynges can produce purring frequencies without neural input, Current Biology (PMID 37794583)
facts.caveat: Measured on excised larynges.

facts.claim: Adult Asian elephants have a resting heart rate around 30 bpm (37 standing adult females averaged 30, range 22-39); a 2024 study of captive elephants estimated mean rates of about 27-38 bpm depending on season and time of day.
facts.figure: avg 30 bpm, range 22-39 bpm (37 adult females standing, Benedict & Lee 1936 as cited); 2024 model-estimated means 26.96-38.22 bpm
facts.source_title: Heart rate patterns of captive Asian elephant in Xishuangbanna, Heliyon 2024 10(4):e25720 (PMC10867636)
facts.caveat: 30 bpm is a 1936 value cited in the paper.

facts.claim: Conscious lab mice measured by telemetry have baseline heart rates of roughly 545-630 beats per minute.
facts.figure: males 544.8 +/- 16.2, females 630.1 +/- 7.9 beats/min (PMID 15626687); 547-567 beats/min (PMID 16399858)
facts.source_title: Xue et al. 2005, Sex differences in the development of angiotensin II-induced hypertension in conscious mice, Am J Physiol Heart Circ Physiol (PMID 15626687)
facts.caveat: Second figure from Fryer et al. 2006 (PMID 16399858).

facts.claim: A blue whale's heart can slow to as low as 2 beats per minute on a dive, with after-dive surface rates of 25 to 37 bpm.
facts.figure: as low as 2 bpm; 25 to 37 bpm after dives
facts.source_title: Goldbogen et al. 2019, Extreme bradycardia and tachycardia in the world's largest animal, PNAS (PMID 31767746)
facts.caveat: Single tagged whale.

facts.claim: People's natural (spontaneous) tapping tempo slows with age: children 4-7 tap every 300-400 ms (~150-200 bpm), adults every 500-600 ms (~100-120 bpm), older adults about every 700 ms (~86 bpm).
facts.figure: children 4-7: 300-400 ms (source says '200 bpm'; actually 150-200 bpm); adults 500-600 ms (=100-120 bpm, computed); older adults ~700 ms (~86 bpm)
facts.source_title: Rose et al. 2020, J Movement Disorders 13(1):47-56 (PMC6987525), citing McAuley et al. 2006, Drake et al. 2000, Vanneste et al. 2001
facts.caveat: Secondary summary; source rounds 300-400 ms to '200 bpm'. Overlaps tba-09/tba-10 (which give children 2-7 at 120-150 bpm), so sources disagree on the child range; use 'about' wording.

facts.claim: At the peak of its growth, Tyrannosaurus rex gained about 2.1 kg per day. It reached skeletal maturity in about two decades and lived up to 28 years.
facts.figure: max growth rate 2.1 kg/day; skeletal maturity ~20 years; lifespan up to 28 years
facts.source_title: Erickson et al. 2004, Gigantism and comparative life-history parameters of tyrannosaurid dinosaurs, Nature 430:772-775 (abstract on RePEc/IDEAS)
facts.caveat: Small sample estimate.

facts.claim: T. rex's big growth spurt started at about age 14 and lasted about four years. Growth stopped at about age 18. During the spurt it gained more than 2 kg per day on average.
facts.figure: spurt from ~14 years, 4 years long, growth stops ~18 years; >2 kg/day average
facts.source_title: Science News: Growth Spurt: Teenage tyrannosaurs packed on the pounds (reporting Erickson et al. 2004)
facts.caveat: End of growth 18-19 depending on source.

facts.claim: Smaller tyrannosaur relatives (Albertosaurus, Gorgosaurus, Daspletosaurus) had a similar four-year growth spurt but gained only about 310-480 g per day.
facts.figure: 310-480 g/day (Science News: 0.3-0.5 kg/day) vs T. rex ~2.1 kg/day
facts.source_title: ScienceBlog press release on Erickson et al. 2004 (also Science News)
facts.caveat: Secondary press coverage.

facts.claim: SUE, the Field Museum's T. rex, lived to about 28 years, the upper end of a T. rex's life expectancy, and reached full size at age 19.
facts.figure: ~28 years lifespan; full size at 19
facts.source_title: Field Museum: SUE the T. rex
facts.caveat: Ages from bone growth rings.

facts.claim: SUE is the most complete T. rex, about 90 percent complete: the museum has 250 of the roughly 380 known bones in a T. rex skeleton. SUE is more than 40 feet long and 13 feet tall at the hip.
facts.figure: ~90% complete; 250 of ~380 bones; >40 ft (~12.3 m) long; 13 ft (~4 m) at hip
facts.source_title: Field Museum: SUE the T. rex
facts.caveat: Do not combine 250/380 and 90% in one line.

facts.claim: T. rex had about 60 saw-edged, pointed teeth, and single teeth reached up to 20 cm long.
facts.figure: 60 teeth; up to 20 cm each
facts.source_title: Natural History Museum (London) Dino Directory: Tyrannosaurus
facts.caveat: Tooth count varies between individuals.

facts.claim: An adult T. rex was usually about 12 m long and probably weighed 5,000-7,000 kg. The largest known individuals, SUE and Scotty, weighed over 8,000 kg. T. rex lived 68-66 million years ago.
facts.figure: ~12 m; 5,000-7,000 kg typical; >8,000 kg largest; 68-66 Ma
facts.source_title: Natural History Museum (London) Dino Directory: Tyrannosaurus
facts.caveat: Mass estimates differ between studies.

facts.claim: Adult T. rex was probably a fast walker, not a runner. The NHM estimates its top speed at around 22 km/h. A 2017 bone-stress model found true running would overload its skeleton and put its maximum speed at about 7.7 m/s (~28 km/h) even under high stress limits.
facts.figure: NHM ~22 km/h; Sellers et al. 2017 max 7.7 m/s (~28 km/h) under high stress limit, walking gaits only; earlier estimates 5-15 m/s
facts.source_title: Sellers et al. 2017, PeerJ 5:e3420 (PMC5518979); NHM Dino Directory: Tyrannosaurus
facts.caveat: Model-dependent; earlier studies estimated 5-15 m/s.

facts.claim: Computer models estimate an adult T. rex's maximum bite at 35,000-57,000 newtons at its back teeth. That is about ten times an alligator's bite and more than four times past estimates.
facts.figure: 35,000-57,000 N; ~10x modern alligator; >4x past estimates
facts.source_title: National Geographic (2012) reporting Bates & Falkingham 2012, Biology Letters 8:20120056
facts.caveat: Model-based.

facts.claim: Stegosaurus had a very small brain for its body. Guinness World Records calls it walnut-sized at about 70 g, and the NHM says it was about the size of a plum. The body was up to about 9 m long, and Guinness gives a weight of about 3.3 tonnes.
facts.figure: brain ~70 g (Guinness, walnut-sized); NHM 'size of a plum'; body ~9 m; ~3.3 t (Guinness)
facts.source_title: Guinness World Records: Smallest-brained dinosaurs; NHM Dino Directory: Stegosaurus
facts.caveat: Walnut vs plum comparisons differ. NHM: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/dino-directory/stegosaurus.html

facts.claim: Daily growth lines in embryo teeth show dinosaur eggs took a long time to hatch: nearly 3 months for Protoceratops (194 g eggs) and about 6 months for Hypacrosaurus (eggs over 4 kg). Bird eggs hatch in 11-85 days.
facts.figure: Protoceratops ~3 months; Hypacrosaurus ~6 months; birds 11-85 days
facts.source_title: Erickson et al. 2017 PNAS 114(3):540-545, via ScienceDaily release
facts.caveat: Two species, few embryos.

facts.claim: Guinness lists the largest known dinosaur eggs as those of the titanosaur Hypselosaurus priscus from France: about 30 cm long and 25.5 cm across, holding about 3.3 litres.
facts.figure: 30 cm long, 255 mm diameter, 3.3 L capacity
facts.source_title: Guinness World Records: Largest dinosaur eggs
facts.caveat: Old record (1961 find).

facts.claim: The earliest well-documented dinosaur fossils, such as Herrerasaurus and Eoraptor, come from Argentina's Ischigualasto Formation and are about 230 million years old. The AMNH notes the very first dinosaur probably lived earlier than any fossil we have.
facts.figure: ~230 Ma (Ischigualasto Formation dated about 231.4-225.9 Ma)
facts.source_title: AMNH: What is the earliest known dinosaur?
facts.caveat: AMNH page 403; checked via search snippets. Dates differ by a few million years.

facts.claim: Nyasasaurus parringtoni from Tanzania, about 245 million years old, is either the earliest known dinosaur or its closest relative. It was 2-3 m long. Its fossils were collected in the 1930s and held at London's Natural History Museum for decades before the 2012/2013 description.
facts.figure: ~245 Ma (CSMonitor; paper: late Anisian, Middle Triassic); 2-3 m long; collected 1930s; dinosaur origins possibly ~15 Myr earlier
facts.source_title: Nesbitt et al. 2013, The oldest dinosaur? A Middle Triassic dinosauriform from Tanzania, Biology Letters (PMC3565515); Christian Science Monitor 2012
facts.caveat: Authors unsure it is a true dinosaur.

facts.claim: Dippy, the Natural History Museum's Diplodocus cast, is made of 292 bones. Andrew Carnegie gave it to the museum in 1905. The NHM lists Diplodocus at 26 m long and 15,000 kg.
facts.figure: 292 bones; given in 1905; Diplodocus 26 m, 15,000 kg (NHM)
facts.source_title: NHM Dino Directory: Diplodocus
facts.caveat: Cast length 21.3 m unverified; removed.

facts.claim: The AMNH's Titanosaur (Patagotitan mayorum) is 122 ft (37.2 m) long, the museum's largest dinosaur on display. The animal weighed about 70 tons, more than 10 African elephants.
facts.figure: 122 ft / 37.2 m; ~70 tons (>10 African elephants)
facts.source_title: AMNH (tumblr.amnh.org): Meet the Titanosaur
facts.caveat: Weight estimates vary (about 57-70 t).

facts.claim: Most paleontologists regard birds as living dinosaurs, because they descend from the common ancestor of all dinosaurs. There are over 10,000 living bird species (the Smithsonian cites about 11,145).
facts.figure: Smithsonian NMNH ~11,145 species; AMNH educator guide 'perhaps as many as 18,000'
facts.source_title: AMNH: Birds: Living Dinosaurs; Smithsonian NMNH Division of Birds (About)
facts.caveat: Pages checked via search snippets; count depends on taxonomy.
